title: A/B Testing & Experimentation
summary: Designing a controlled experiment, sample size/power, and the classic pitfalls (peeking, novelty effect, Simpson's paradox) that turn a clean test into a wrong conclusion.

slides.markdown:
An **A/B test** splits users into a **control** group (existing experience) and a **treatment** group (the new variant), then compares a metric between them. The **randomization unit** — what actually gets randomly assigned (individual user, session, or account) — must be chosen so units don't leak between groups: randomizing by session when users span multiple sessions can let the same user see both variants, contaminating the comparison.

Everything downstream — sample size, significance testing — assumes this split was done cleanly and randomly.

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing a metric and minimum detectable effect
slides.markdown:
The **primary metric** should be a direct, pre-registered measure of the outcome you actually care about (e.g. conversion rate, not a proxy that could move without truly reflecting user value). The **minimum detectable effect (MDE)** is the smallest true effect size you want the test to reliably catch.

The MDE choice directly trades off against sample size and runtime: demanding the test detect a tiny 0.1% lift requires far more traffic than detecting a 5% lift — setting the MDE too small can make a test practically un-runnable within a reasonable timeframe.

**Statistical power** is the probability of detecting a true effect if one exists (`1-β`, the complement of Type II error from [statistical-inference](statistical-inference)). Required sample size grows with a smaller MDE, a lower baseline rate, and higher desired power (commonly 80%).

**Underpowered tests** are the silent killer of A/B programs — too few users and a "no significant difference" result doesn't mean no effect; it often just means the test never had a real chance of detecting the effect that was there.

**Wrong belief:** "I'll check results daily and stop as soon as I see significance — saves time." **Why it's wrong:** repeated checking and stopping at the first significant-looking moment inflates the **false positive rate** far above nominal `α` — a truly-null test will eventually cross the line by pure random fluctuation.

**Correct model:** decide sample size (or duration) **in advance**, evaluate significance only once, or use a sequential method built for valid early stopping — not ad-hoc peeking.

A **novelty effect** is a temporary spike in engagement simply because something is *new* and users are curious — it fades as the change becomes routine, meaning early results can overstate the long-run impact. A **primacy effect** is the opposite: existing users resist a familiar-feature change out of habit, understating the eventual impact once they adjust.

Both argue for running tests long enough to see behavior stabilize, and for treating very early results (especially from a fresh cohort of first-time exposures) with appropriate skepticism rather than as the final verdict.

**Simpson's paradox**: an effect can reverse when data splits into subgroups vs. aggregate. Treatment can *win* overall while *losing* every segment — driven by unbalanced segment sizes between groups.

![Simpson's paradox: loses per segment, wins in aggregate](assets/simpsons-paradox.svg)

The fix: check whether **segment composition differs between control and treatment** before trusting an aggregate.

assets.alt: Simpson's paradox: treatment loses in every segment individually but wins in the misleading aggregate

slides.markdown:
The core assumption behind A/B testing (**SUTVA**) is that one user's assignment doesn't affect another's outcome. **Network effects** break this: a treatment user's new behavior can spill over onto control-group friends, contaminating the comparison.

The fix for network-effect-prone features is usually **cluster randomization** — randomizing entire connected groups (region, friend-cluster) instead of individuals, so spillover stays within one variant group.

| Signal | Trust it? |
|---|---|
| Pre-registered primary metric hit significance at planned sample size | Yes |
| A secondary metric out of 30 tracked happened to hit p<0.05 | Question it — multiple-testing risk |
| Result appeared significant on day 2 of a planned 14-day test | Question it — peeking risk |
| Segment breakdown shows the effect reverses in a major segment | Investigate — possible Simpson's paradox |

Decide *how* you'll read the dashboard **before** the test starts (which metric, what sample size, how long) — reading it opportunistically after the fact is exactly how peeking and multiple-testing problems creep in unnoticed.

slides.subTitle: Optional stopping vs sequential testing
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "a fixed-sample-size test and a sequential (early-stopping-aware) test both just check p < 0.05, so I can switch between them mid-test without consequence." **Why it's wrong:** a fixed-sample test's `p < 0.05` guarantee only holds if you evaluate significance **once**, at the pre-planned sample size — peeking with that same threshold, at multiple checkpoints, is exactly the inflated-false-positive problem from earlier. A true sequential method (e.g. sequential probability ratio test, always-valid p-values) uses a **different, stricter** boundary specifically designed to stay valid under repeated looks.

**Correct model:** decide *before the test starts* which framework you're using — fixed-horizon (commit to one look) or sequential (use its specific stopping rule) — and never borrow the other framework's threshold. Mixing them is a subtler version of peeking, not a safe shortcut.
